title: ASME Stamp Audit Support in Baton Rouge, LA | NDE
description: Baton Rouge vessel, exchanger and spool shops: Level III help with the NDE side of an ASME or R-stamp review, owner specs and records. Ask for a gap review.
h1: ASME Code Stamp Audit Support for Baton Rouge Fabricators: Getting the NDE Program Review-Ready
html:
Baton Rouge vessel, heat exchanger and piping-spool shops live between two sets of rules: the ASME Code their certificate covers, and the purchase specifications of the refineries and chemical plants they sell to. If your ASME Certificate of Authorization or National Board R certificate review is coming up, Atlantis NDT, an ASNT NDT Level III consulting firm, gets the NDE part of your quality control system ready: written practice, Section V procedures, examiner files, outside-lab control and the records behind every stamped job. Tell us your review date and the designators involved; we reply within one business day.

The river corridor and the equipment it buys

The stretch of the Mississippi from Baton Rouge down toward New Orleans holds one of the densest groupings of refineries and chemical plants in the country, and it consumes pressure equipment without pause. Exchanger bundles get re-tubed, drums and columns get new nozzles, reactors get repaired at every turnaround, and capital projects bring in new vessels and miles of process piping. The fabricators that serve this market tend to fall into three groups:

  • Vessel and exchanger shops holding a U designator, building shell-and-tube exchangers, separators, drums and filter housings to Section VIII Division 1, with a few working to Division 2 for heavier service.
  • Repair organizations holding the National Board R certificate, some of them shop-based and many of them working inside plant fences during outages.
  • Spool and module fabricators building process piping under ASME B31.3, a code that carries no Certification Mark; owners commonly require the same quality control discipline and send their own auditors to check it, so the spool line often runs under the same manual as the stamped vessel work.

Gulf Coast conditions also shape the NDE work itself. Much of the examination happens in open yards or on equipment that sat in summer sun, where steel surface temperature can climb past the standard temperature range in Section V Article 6 for penetrant examination; outside that range the procedure has to be qualified at the actual temperature, and the record should show the temperature was checked. Fluorescent magnetic particle work needs a darkened area that a bright yard does not provide, and heavy rain and humidity work against clean, dry surfaces for both methods. A review team that sees outdoor examinations in your job files will ask how your procedures handled those conditions.

Every one of those groups gets audited from two directions: by the ASME or National Board review team, and by the owner's supplier-quality people who want to see the plant's specifications honored. The NDE program has to satisfy both without contradicting itself.

Louisiana's rules: boilers regulated, vessels driven by the owner

Louisiana's boiler law is administered by the Office of State Fire Marshal, through the section the National Board lists as the Mechanical Safety Section and the state code calls the Boiler Inspection Section, headquartered in Baton Rouge under a chief boiler inspector. The shape of the Louisiana program is different from many states, and a shop that sells mostly to plants needs to understand why.

  • Boilers are firmly covered. The state adopts the ASME Code as its boiler construction code, National Board registration is required for boilers, and a decal carrying the state serial number goes on each boiler. A "Louisiana Special" (a non-Code boiler) needs the Fire Marshal's approval.
  • Pressure vessels follow the owner. According to the National Board's synopsis of state laws, Section VIII construction applies in Louisiana when the owner or user requires it. The state's own definitions also exempt evaporators, heat exchangers and vessels that form part of a larger chemical or petroleum processing system from jurisdictional inspection.
  • Shop reviews still happen here. The Fire Marshal's office lists ASME and National Board shop reviews for Certificates of Authorization among its services, so a Louisiana shop can expect a state representative to have a role at review time. Confirm with your Authorized Inspection Agency who will attend.
  • Repairs go to the NBIC. The National Board Inspection Code is adopted for repairs and alterations, and insurance-company inspectors are accepted in place of state deputies. Power boilers tied to continuous processes can have their internal inspection interval extended with approval, which shapes when repair work lands.

So for most of what a Baton Rouge vessel shop builds, the state is not the party demanding a U stamp; the plant is. The owner's specification, its insurer and its mechanical integrity program under OSHA's process safety management standard are what drive Code construction and National Board registration on process vessels. That makes the purchase order and the specifications attached to it as important to your NDE program as the Code itself.

Two rulebooks on every job: the Code and the plant specification

Refinery and chemical-plant specifications routinely ask for more examination than the Code minimum. Common additions we see on Gulf Coast purchase orders:

  • Full volumetric examination of welds the Code would allow to be spot examined, or radiography of joints the Code would accept without it.
  • Ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, but only to an owner-approved procedure and by examiners the owner has accepted.
  • Owner review of NDE procedures before work starts, sometimes with a Level III signature required on each one.
  • Magnetic particle or penetrant examination of nozzle welds, attachment welds and weld preps beyond what Division 1 asks.
  • Positive material identification and hardness testing. These are owner requirements rather than Section V methods, but they often get routed through the same NDE paperwork.
  • Specific report formats, a required NDE map for each vessel, and a turnover package delivered with the data report.

The trap is a QC manual that only knows the Code. When the job file shows 100 percent ultrasonic examination while your manual and procedures only describe spot radiography, an ASME reviewer will ask what controlled that work, and an owner auditor will ask why your procedure was not on their approved list. The fix is a manual section that says how purchaser requirements are reviewed at contract stage, how added examinations are planned and assigned, which procedure covers them, and how the record shows both Code and specification were met.

What turnaround repair work does to an NDE program

R certificate holders in this region often do their most important work during a plant outage, under schedule pressure, on equipment that cannot leave the site. The NDE side of that work has a few predictable weak points.

  • Original code of construction. The NBIC requires repairs to meet the code the item was built to, so a repair to an older vessel may call for examination rules from an earlier edition. The repair plan should say which edition and which paragraph governs each examination.
  • Crew substitution. Outside NDE companies swap technicians between shifts and sites during a turnaround. Each examiner who touches an R job needs a certification your system has accepted, not just the one the lab sent on day one.
  • Two inspectors. The plant's inspector (often an owner-user inspection organization or the insurer's inspector) has to accept the repair, and your Authorized Inspector has to sign the R form. Both read the NDE reports.
  • Records that leave with the crew. Field reports written on the lab's own forms and kept in its truck are a common gap. The R-form package should carry the examination records in a form your shop controls.

The NBIC side of this is covered in more depth on our R-stamp NDE audit support page and in our guide to NBIC audit preparation.

What the review team pulls from your NDE files

ASME's description of the joint review has the team reading your manual before it visits, then judging how well you carry it out on real Code work or on a mock-up that will never be stamped. For a Baton Rouge exchanger shop the demonstration often centres on a shell-side or channel weld that calls for volumetric examination, a nozzle attachment that calls for MT or PT, and the hydrostatic test. The team will expect:

  1. A written practice, in the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition your Code edition references, that covers every method your shop performs and the rules for accepting examiners from outside companies.
  2. Section V procedures for each method, approved by a Level III, with technique details on the shop floor where examiners can use them. The relevant articles are Article 2 for radiography, Article 4 for ultrasonic examination of welds, Article 6 for penetrant and Article 7 for magnetic particle.
  3. For bought-in NDE, the subcontractor's procedure and personnel qualification files available on site. ASME's joint review guidance is explicit that those records must be available to the team where the review takes place.
  4. Evidence that someone in your company reviewed the outside reports and radiographs before the Authorized Inspector saw them.
  5. Calibration and verification records for gauges, yokes, ultrasonic instruments and reference blocks used on Code work.
  6. For a renewal, records for every Code job on the list you submit, including field work.

Atlantis performs no radiography in the United States. Radiographs on Code jobs here are made by a licensed radiography company; what we can do is review the film or digital images, the technique and the report as a Level III, and help you write the requirements your shop places on that company.

Atlantis's role for Baton Rouge shops

Baton Rouge is within driving range of Atlantis's Houston office, which makes repeat site visits practical when a shop wants them; the document work itself is done remotely. The usual scope:

  • Gap assessment of the NDE sections of the QC manual against the Code edition in force and against your largest customers' specifications.
  • Drafting or revising the written practice and the Section V procedures, including UT procedures written to satisfy an owner's ultrasonic-in-lieu-of-radiography requirements.
  • Level III approval of procedures and technique sheets, and Level III examinations for your examiners under your written practice, with your company signing each certification.
  • Building the acceptance file for each outside NDE company and the purchaser-requirements section of the manual.
  • A mock review on the demonstration item and a records walkthrough with the people who will face the team.
  • Help closing findings afterwards, from root cause to the corrective-action evidence your Authorized Inspection Agency wants to see.

For broader Level III services in the city, see NDT consulting in Baton Rouge and our Level III of record service for Baton Rouge. Plants that need in-service examination rather than audit preparation should look at pressure vessel inspection services in Baton Rouge.

Lines Atlantis does not cross

We prepare you for the review; we do not conduct it. The ASME team leader, your Authorized Inspection Agency and, where present, the state's representative judge your system, and ASME decides on the certificate. Atlantis is not an Authorized Inspection Agency and holds no authority to sign data reports or R forms. Your company owns its manual, and its quality manager decides what goes into it. Your company also certifies its own NDE personnel; our Level III examinations feed your decision, they do not replace it.

Welding is the other boundary. WPS, PQR and welder performance qualification under Section IX belong to your welding engineer, and Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures; the WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer sets out what that program has to show. Nuclear work is not part of our service at all: no Section III, no N-type certificates and no NQA-1 programs.

Baton Rouge readiness checklist for the NDE portion

  • A contract-review step in the manual that captures owner NDE requirements on every purchase order and turns them into an examination plan.
  • Procedures that cover every examination your customers actually order, including the UT-in-lieu-of-RT work and the added MT or PT on nozzles.
  • An approved-subcontractor list naming each NDE company, the methods you accept it for, and the date its file was last reviewed.
  • For each subcontractor, a current file in your office: written practice, certifications for every examiner it sends, its procedures with your review recorded, and equipment calibration evidence.
  • A way to accept substitute technicians during turnarounds before they examine an R job.
  • Repair plans that state the original code of construction and the examination paragraph that governs each repair weld.
  • NDE reports that identify joint, procedure, examiner, technique, result and acceptance reference, on forms your shop controls.
  • A person in your company assigned to review outside reports and radiographs, with the qualification your manual requires for that review.
  • Calibration due dates for every gauge, yoke, flaw detector and reference block used on Code work, with nothing overdue in service.
  • A demonstration item, or a live job, that exercises the NDE methods in your scope and leaves a complete record trail to the data report.
  • Owner audit reports from the past year reviewed for NDE findings, since a review team may ask what you did about them.

What to send us

A gap assessment starts from your written practice, the NDE chapters of the quality control manual, the current procedure list with revision levels, a sample of three examiner certification files, the acceptance files for your NDE subcontractors, your calibration register, and one recent job package, ideally a vessel or repair that carried an owner's added NDE requirements. If your review is a renewal, add the list of Code work you plan to submit. Our NDT audit documentation page shows how we organize that evidence, and the national ASME audit support guide covers the review process in more detail. Shops whose examiners need method training can look at NDT training for Baton Rouge.

faq.q: Does Louisiana require our pressure vessels to be ASME stamped?
faq.a: The National Board's synopsis of Louisiana law shows Section VIII construction applying when the owner or user requires it, and the state's definitions exempt heat exchangers and vessels within larger processing systems from jurisdictional inspection. In practice the plants buying your vessels almost always require the stamp and National Board registration in their specifications.

faq.q: Who attends a joint review for a shop in Baton Rouge?
faq.a: An ASME team leader and your Authorized Inspection Agency, and the Louisiana Fire Marshal's office lists shop reviews for Certificates of Authorization among its services. Ask your AIA early who will be on the team so there are no surprises about scheduling.

faq.q: Our customer wants UT instead of radiography. What does the review team need to see?
faq.a: A UT procedure that meets the Section V and construction-code requirements for that use, examiners qualified for it under your written practice, and records showing the examination followed the procedure. If the owner also approves procedures and examiners, keep that approval in the job file. See our procedure development page.

faq.q: Can Atlantis act as our Level III?
faq.a: Yes, as an outside agency Level III for UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, if your written practice provides for it. We approve procedures, give Level III examinations and review results; your company keeps the authority to certify its examiners.

faq.q: Do B31.3 spools need to be covered by our QC manual?
faq.a: B31.3 piping carries no ASME Certification Mark, so the review team is focused on your stamped scope. Owners, though, often require B31.3 work to run under the same quality system, and their auditors will check it. Many shops cover both in one manual. Our ASME B31.3 page summarizes the examination rules.

faq.q: Will Atlantis take radiographs for our turnaround repairs?
faq.a: No. In the United States Atlantis does not take radiographs at all; a licensed radiography company does. We can review the radiographs, the technique and the reports as a Level III and help you control that subcontractor.

faq.q: How do we handle NDE technicians swapped in mid-turnaround?
faq.a: Write an acceptance step into the manual: before a substitute examines an R job, someone authorized checks the certification and method against your accepted list and records it. Our training records and certificates page covers the paperwork.

faq.q: Do you write our WPS and PQR documents?
faq.a: No. The welding program belongs to your welding engineer, and Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures. We keep strictly to the NDE side of the quality system.

faq.q: What if the team writes NDE findings during the review?
faq.a: Some can be closed during the review itself. For the rest we help you trace the cause, correct documents or records, and put together the corrective-action evidence your AIA and the team leader need. ASME makes the final decision on the certificate.

faq.q: Do you help with nuclear certificates?
faq.a: No. Nuclear construction is not work we take on: no Section III fabrication, no N-type certificates and no NQA-1 programs.
